card: Will you stand by your Slav brothers, or sign the order to mobilize?
intro: You are Nicholas II, Emperor of Russia, aged 46. Under the Fundamental Laws of 1906, the direction of foreign policy, the power to declare war and make peace, and supreme command of the army and navy all rest with you, and the Duma (parliament) has no say in foreign affairs. Beside you are Sergei Sazonov, an emotional Foreign Minister; War Minister Vladimir Sukhomlinov; Nikolai Yanushkevich, who became Chief of the General Staff in March; and Alexander Krivoshein, the Minister of Agriculture, whose voice carries the most weight in the Council of Ministers. Russia’s ally is France, and Serbia, a fellow Orthodox Slav nation, looks to Russia as its protector. At the summer palace at Peterhof are Empress Alexandra, your four daughters and Alexei, the nine-year-old heir, who suffers from hemophilia.

RU-00.title: Shots in Sarajevo

map.caption: Princip and Grabež received pistols and bombs in Belgrade and crossed the Drina into Bosnia near Loznica.

telegram.text: Heir to the throne Archduke Franz Ferdinand and wife shot dead in Sarajevo / Assassin a Bosnian Serb student

RU-00.event: On the morning of Sunday 28 June, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie were shot dead in Sarajevo, in Bosnia. The Vienna newspapers soon began writing that the plot had been hatched in Belgrade. The Serbian government strongly condemned the crime and declared that if accomplices were found in Serbia, they would be brought to trial.
RU-00.scene: The day before, you had visited the British battlecruiser squadron at Kronstadt and toured Admiral Beatty’s flagship, the Lion. On 28 June you went to Mass with your daughters, paddled a kayak alongside Alexei and in the evening swam in the sea; your diary for the day does not mention Sarajevo at all. Two days later you received Sukhomlinov, Grand Duke Nicholas Nikolaevich and Sazonov in turn, and that evening Rasputin spent time with the family. Nicholas Hartwig, the Russian minister in Belgrade, is known to be very close to Prime Minister Pašić, and Vienna regards him as the man behind Serbia’s hard line.

voices.text: Your Majesty, there is no evidence whatsoever that the Serbian government had any part in this crime. Russia must not let Vienna turn one young man’s crime into the guilt of the whole Serbian nation.

Custom between monarchies requires that Your Majesty send condolences to the imperial house in Vienna and that the court go into mourning. Your Majesty must also choose the envoys to send to the funeral.

voices.who: Nekludoff (former Russian minister in Sofia, later recalling Hartwig)
voices.text: He was a true and faithful friend of the Serbians; he was just as sincere and ardent a Russian patriot.

choices.text: Have Hartwig press Pašić to investigate accomplices in Serbia himself and report to Vienna, before Vienna can seize on a pretext
choices.why: Serbia must move first if Vienna is to be left without a pretext
choices.after: Pašić received the Russian advice courteously, but even his government found it hard to touch Apis, the head of military intelligence, and his secret society, the Black Hand. All that reached Vienna was word that a few frontier guard officers had been questioned.

choices.text: Send condolences and declare court mourning, but reject the Vienna papers’ claim that the Serbian government is to blame
choices.why: Keep the courtesies, but do not let Serbia be cast as the culprit
choices.realNote: The Russian government offered condolences but did not accept the Viennese press’s claim that the Serbian government was involved in the assassination. There is no record that the Emperor gave separate instructions on the matter, and Sarajevo does not appear in his diary.
choices.after: The Russian court declared mourning. Royal houses across Europe wanted to send representatives to the funeral, but Vienna, citing the old emperor’s health, declined foreign delegations, and the archduke and his wife were quietly buried at Artstetten Castle on 4 July. Investigators in Vienna, meanwhile, were already taking down statements that the Sarajevo assassins had been armed in Belgrade.

choices.text: As Fredericks advises, keep to the courtesies between monarchies, say little about Serbia, and leave it to Vienna and Belgrade
choices.why: Step early into another’s quarrel and it is hard to step out again
choices.after: Pan-Slav newspapers attacked the government for its silence, and Hartwig wrote to his old colleagues in St Petersburg to air his discontent.

note.text: Nekludoff, who had been minister in Sofia, recalled that Hartwig, working through old colleagues inside the Foreign Ministry, had reshaped even Sazonov’s Balkan policy. No evidence has emerged, however, that Hartwig knew of the Black Hand’s plan to assassinate the archduke.

RU-00a.place: Islands off the Finnish coast, imperial yacht Standart / Foreign Ministry, St Petersburg
RU-00a.title: Ambassador Szápáry Returns

telegram.text: Italian ambassador Carlotti to Baron Schilling / Austria capable of irrevocable step against Serbia / Vienna seems to believe Russia will protest only in words / Russia would do well to make plain representation to Vienna directly

RU-00a.event: On 10 July Nicholas Hartwig, the Russian minister in Belgrade, called on the Austrian minister Giesl, just back from leave, and collapsed and died on the spot. Two days later, on 12 July, Rasputin, who had gone home to Pokrovskoye in Siberia, was stabbed in the stomach by a woman named Khioniya Guseva and taken to hospital in Tyumen. On 14 July, after attending the consecration at Kronstadt of a new dry dock named after Alexei, you set off with your family aboard the Standart for the islands off the Finnish coast.
RU-00a.scene: With the yacht anchored among the islands, you spend your days kayaking and swimming with the officers. On 18 July a courier arrives with a load of papers. In the capital, meanwhile, at Countess Kleinmichel’s evening party on 16 July, the Italian ambassador Carlotti had hinted to Baron Schilling, chief of the foreign minister’s chancellery, that Vienna might take an irrevocable step against Serbia in the belief that Russia would protest only in words. Sazonov, who had spent a few days in the country, returned to the capital on the morning of 18 July, heard this along with a telegram from Shebeko, the ambassador in Vienna, and resolved to give Austria a firm warning. But soon afterward he met the Austrian ambassador Szápáry, just back from leave, and changed his mind: Szápáry had assured him, with complete conviction, that Austria had no intention at all of making relations with Serbia more acute.

voices.who: Baron Schilling (chief of the foreign minister’s chancellery, to Carlotti on 16 July)
voices.text: Russia will never tolerate any infringement by Austria of Serbia’s integrity and independence. But if Russia says so to Vienna directly, it may sound like an ultimatum. It would be better for Austria’s allies, Italy and Germany, to counsel Vienna.
If that is Russia’s firm determination, it would be well to make it plain to Vienna directly. Vienna believes that Russia may protest, but will not defend Serbia by force.
Ambassador Szápáry says Austria has no intention whatever of pressing Serbia hard. There is no reason to make idle threats and provoke the hard-liners in Vienna.

choices.text: Take Schilling’s view that Vienna’s allies must restrain it: send Wilhelm a private telegram asking him frankly what Vienna plans
choices.why: Only Germany, Vienna’s ally, is in a position to stop it
choices.after: Wilhelm was cruising off Norway, and the Foreign Office in Berlin prepared a reply saying that Germany did not know the details of Vienna’s plans. All your telegram left behind was a suspicion that Berlin was hiding Vienna’s timetable.

choices.text: On Carlotti’s advice, have the Vienna embassy warn formally that Russia will move troops if Serbia’s independence is harmed
choices.why: Only an early, plain warning can stop Vienna from misjudging Russia
choices.after: Berchtold received the warning politely but did not change the wording of the ultimatum. Vienna did, however, report to Berlin that this time Russia might not back down.

choices.text: Trust Szápáry’s assurances of peace, and send Vienna only a short, mild warning telegram during Poincaré’s visit
choices.why: Needless threats would only provoke the hard-liners in Vienna
choices.realNote: This judgment was Sazonov’s, and there is no record that the Emperor gave instructions of his own. The warning telegram sent to Vienna on 22 July was indeed short, asking only that the dangerous consequences be pointed out ‘in a friendly but firm manner’.
choices.after: Sazonov told Schilling there had been no need even for threats: “He was as gentle as a lamb.” On the afternoon of 19 July you left the yacht at Kronstadt and returned to Peterhof. At 4 a.m. on 22 July Sazonov sent the embassy in Vienna a short telegram asking it to point out ‘in a friendly but firm manner’ the dangerous consequences of any action of an unacceptable character with regard to the dignity of Serbia.

note.text: Shebeko’s telegram No. 88, which Sazonov learned of from Schilling on 18 July, was not included in the official collection the Russian government published (the Orange Book), and its contents are unknown. Nor is it known whether the Italian ambassador passed Schilling’s words on to Rome.

pressure.title: Two People Far Away
pressure.text: On the evening of 30 June Rasputin again spent time with your family at Peterhof. Soon afterward he left for his home in Siberia, where he was stabbed on 12 July; he now lies in hospital in Tyumen. In early July Alexei complained of nausea and back pain and ran a fever for several days. Whenever her son falls ill, the Empress turns to Rasputin’s prayers.

RU-01.title: Four Days with Poincaré
RU-01.event: At 2 p.m. sharp on 20 July the French battleships France and Jean Bart entered the roads at Kronstadt. The same day, in St Petersburg, strikes were spreading in protest against the police shooting at a meeting of Putilov factory workers on 16 July. By then more than 100,000 workers had downed tools (130,000 to 150,000, by some accounts).
RU-01.scene: You met President Poincaré aboard the imperial yacht and brought him to Peterhof, and for four days now gun salutes, banquets and reviews have followed one another. At the reception for the diplomatic corps in the Winter Palace on 21 July, Poincaré gave the Austrian ambassador Szápáry a pointed warning over Serbia. On the evening of 22 July the grand ducal couple gave a dinner in a tent at the Krasnoe Selo camp. Anastasia, a daughter of the King of Montenegro and wife of your father’s cousin Grand Duke Nicholas Nikolaevich, decorated the table with Lorraine thistles and prophesied war, falling silent only when she caught your eye. Around then, in the Vyborg district of the capital, striking workers were putting up barricades and fighting the police. There are rumors that Vienna is preparing something against Serbia, but no one at Peterhof knows what.

voices.who: Poincaré (French President, to Ambassador Szápáry on 21 July)
voices.text: With a little good will this Serbian business is easy to settle. But it can just as easily become acute. Serbia has some very warm friends in the Russian people. And Russia has an ally, France.

voices.who: Grand Duchess Anastasia (to Ambassador Paléologue at the dinner on 22 July, as he recalled it)
voices.text: There’s going to be war. There’ll be nothing left of Austria. You’re going to get back Alsace and Lorraine. Our armies will meet in Berlin.
Don’t let the Montenegrin sisters sway you. War would be a disaster for this country, and for our boy.

choices.text: Pledge firm solidarity with Poincaré: if Vienna touches Serbia’s sovereignty, France and Russia will stand against it together
choices.why: Vienna and Berlin will back down only if France and Russia speak as one
choices.after: The two heads of state agreed to act together in Vienna against any demand that would harm Serbia’s sovereignty and independence. On the evening of 23 July, 104 guests sat down to the farewell dinner on the deck of the France beneath her 305 mm guns; by the time it began, the Austrian minister in Belgrade had already handed over the ultimatum (6 p.m. Belgrade time). Vienna had timed the delivery so that the news would spread while Poincaré was at sea.

choices.text: Heed the Empress: tell Poincaré Russia cannot fight before the Great Programme is complete, and propose calming Belgrade together
choices.why: A war fought unready is more dangerous than a disappointed ally
choices.after: Poincaré boarded the France unable to hide his disappointment. Ambassador Paléologue reported to Paris that Russia’s resolve was wavering.

choices.text: After the reception, take Szápáry aside and state flatly that Russia will not stand by if Serbia’s sovereignty is harmed
choices.why: Vienna must not be allowed to treat Russia’s words as empty
choices.after: Stony-faced, Szápáry passed the warning on to Vienna. Berchtold did not change the text, but the signal that Russia was not bluffing reached Berlin as well.

note.text: Russia used the Julian calendar, 13 days behind the Western calendar. Nicholas’s diary records the day Poincaré arrived as ‘7 July’ and the day Germany declared war as ‘19 July’.

RU-02.place: St Petersburg, Foreign Ministry and Council of Ministers
RU-02.title: Council of Ministers: Back Down Again?

telegram.text: Austrian minister Giesl delivered note 6 p.m. 23rd / Time limit 48 hours, expires 6 p.m. 25th / Ten demands / Includes participation of Austrian officials in investigation inside Serbia

RU-02.event: Arriving from Tsarskoe Selo at about 10 a.m., Sazonov heard the news and at once exclaimed, “C’est la guerre européenne!” (“This means a European war”). He reported to you straightaway by telephone, and at 11 a.m. the Austrian ambassador Szápáry came to the Foreign Ministry with a copy of the note.
RU-02.scene: The Council of Ministers has met at 3 p.m. Goremykin, the 74-year-old Prime Minister, takes the chair, and Sazonov recalls how Russia gave way to German pressure in the Bosnian crisis of 1909, warning that if it retreats again it will lose its standing in the Balkans. War Minister Sukhomlinov and Navy Minister Grigorovich admit that the Great Programme of rearmament will not be finished until 1917 and that Russia is not ready for a major war, yet both support firm diplomacy. Finance Minister Bark has to move quickly to withdraw the state deposits held in Germany. The discussion is led by Krivoshein, the minister you trust most.

voices.text: It is true that the rearmament program is not finished, and no one in Russia wants war. But Russia’s position is far better than in 1909. If the government hesitates at this decisive moment, neither public opinion nor the Duma will understand, and excessive concessions have only emboldened Germany and Austria rather than appeasing them. Russia must now speak more firmly.
The Baltic Fleet is not ready to face the German fleet. The four new dreadnoughts have not yet entered service. Be firm in diplomacy, Your Majesty, but war must be avoided.

choices.text: As Spalajković asks, promise Serbia military support and tell Vienna and Berlin Russia will mobilize once the deadline passes
choices.why: Retreat as in 1909 and Russia loses its place in the Balkans
choices.after: Belgrade was elated by the telegram from its minister Spalajković. In Paris, with the President and the Prime Minister at sea, the Foreign Ministry sent a worried telegram warning that Russia was handing Germany a pretext.

choices.text: Heed Grigorovich’s warning on rearmament: urge Serbia to accept almost all of the ultimatum, and put off military preparations
choices.why: Buy time until 1917, even at the price of humiliation
choices.after: Krivoshein put down his pen, his face set, and Sazonov had to see the Serbian minister as soon as the meeting ended. Word that Russia was backing down again, as in 1909, began to spread through the newsrooms of the evening papers.

choices.text: Ask Vienna to extend the deadline, urge Serbia not to resist by force, and ready four districts and the fleets for mobilization
choices.why: Buy time with diplomacy while keeping force ready behind it
choices.after: The Council adopted five resolutions: a request to extend the deadline, advice to Serbia, preparation to mobilize the Kiev, Odessa, Moscow and Kazan military districts and the fleets, the stockpiling of war materials, and the recall of Treasury funds held in Germany and Austria. In approving the resolutions you wrote in your own hand the word ‘Baltic’ before ‘Black Sea Fleet’. Vienna curtly rejected the request for an extension.

note.text: The Council’s resolution proposed advising Serbia that, if it could not defend itself, it should not resist by force but should declare that it was yielding to force and entrust its fate to the judgment of the Great Powers. Russia’s official decision was not to egg Serbia on unconditionally.

pressure.title: A Diplomatic Tsushima
pressure.text: In the Bosnian crisis of 1909 Russia yielded to a virtual German ultimatum, and people likened it to the disastrous defeat in the war with Japan, calling it a ‘diplomatic Tsushima’. The memory of 1905, when defeat led to revolution, also lingers. If Russia backs down again, the criticism of the Duma, the newspapers and the Guard officers will fall on the Emperor.

RU-03.title: The Period Preparatory to War
RU-03.clock: About 8 hours until Serbia’s reply is due
RU-03.scene: You went to Krasnoe Selo in the morning and reviewed the Astrakhan Grenadier Regiment at 10 a.m.; from 11 until noon you are meeting six ministers. On the table, beside the previous day’s Council resolutions, lie the 1913 regulations on the ‘period preparatory to war’. Without a mobilization order, they allow troops at the summer camps to return to their home garrisons, cadets to be commissioned early, frontier guards and fortress garrisons to be strengthened, and the railways to be readied for military use. But the regulations apply not only to the Austrian frontier; they also cover the Warsaw and Vilna military districts, which border Germany. Quartermaster General Danilov, who is responsible for operational planning, is away on a tour of inspection.

voices.text: If Your Majesty proclaims the preparatory period, actual mobilization will come several days sooner. The German army assembles far faster than the Russian. Every day lost means that many more soldiers lost at the frontier.
This is preparation, not mobilization. Because it is not proclaimed publicly, it can show Vienna Russia’s resolve without greatly provoking Berlin.

On Thursday evening Austria presented Serbia with an ultimatum containing demands, 8 of which are unacceptable for an independent state. The time limit expired today at 6 p.m. Naturally, talk everywhere here is about nothing else.

choices.text: Postpone the preparatory period so that Berlin cannot say Russia moved first, and approve partial mobilization only in principle
choices.why: Better to be slow than to be blamed for moving first
choices.after: Yanushkevich protested that every day lost delayed mobilization by as much. The frontier stayed quiet, and the German General Staff reported that Russia was not yet moving.

choices.text: Proclaim the preparatory period in all European Russia from tomorrow; approve partial mobilization of four districts in principle
choices.why: Prepare even a day sooner and fewer soldiers are lost at the frontier
choices.after: At 6 p.m., in front of the mess tent, you commissioned the cadets early, and that night, after watching the theater’s 50th-anniversary performance, you did not get to bed until after 3 a.m. because of the mass of papers. The preparatory period took effect the next day, 26 July. Across the frontier, German intelligence officers soon began reporting suspicious movements on the Russian side.

choices.text: Apply the preparatory period only to southwestern districts such as Kiev and Odessa, to show that Austria alone is the target
choices.why: Show resolve to Vienna and restraint to Berlin at the same time
choices.after: The General Staff objected that the railway network was a single system and hard to divide by region, but the order was carried out only in the southwest. The German frontier stayed quiet.

note.text: In his telegram to Wilhelm of 30 July, Nicholas stated that ‘the military measures which have now come into force were decided five days ago for reasons of defence on account of Austria’s preparations’. The sentence later became a point of dispute over when Russia’s war preparations began.

RU-04.place: St Petersburg, Foreign Ministry on Palace Square
RU-04.title: Direct Talks with Vienna

telegram.text: Serbian reply delivered just before deadline / Minister Giesl left by 6:30 p.m. train / Diplomatic relations broken off / Serbia ordered mobilization at 3 p.m. / Government moving to Niš

RU-04.event: On 25 July, minutes before the deadline, Serbia delivered its reply. It accepted most of the demands but attached reservations to several, and it rejected point 6, under which Austrian officials would take part in judicial inquiries inside Serbia. On 26 July the British Foreign Secretary, Sir Edward Grey, proposed a conference in London of the ambassadors of four powers: Britain, Germany, France and Italy.
RU-04.scene: On the wall of Sazonov’s office hangs a portrait of Chancellor Gorchakov, who in 1870 made light of Germany’s rise. On 26 July Sazonov summons the Austrian ambassador Szápáry, asks for a frank and friendly conversation, and proposes that the two countries jointly revise only those points of the ultimatum that infringe Serbia’s sovereignty. The German ambassador Pourtalès advises that a conference in London would be too cumbersome and that Russia should talk to Vienna directly, while the British ambassador Buchanan asks Russia to support Grey’s conference. In the same streets where barricades stood only days ago, patriotic crowds carrying portraits of the Emperor and the national flag grow larger by the day.

voices.text: A four-power conference is too cumbersome. If Russia truly wants peace, let it talk to Vienna directly. Germany will help with those talks.

If only the few points that infringe Serbia’s sovereignty are revised, Russia will see to it that Serbia accepts almost all the remaining demands. But Russia cannot accept that Serbia be made an Austrian protectorate.
France will fulfill the obligations of the alliance. But avoid giving Germany a pretext. The French government can help Russia only if public opinion stands behind it.

choices.text: Ask Vienna for direct talks to revise the ultimatum’s problem points together, and agree as well to Grey’s four-power conference
choices.why: The more channels kept open, the longer war can be put off
choices.realNote: On 26 July, on Pourtalès’s advice, Sazonov put direct talks first, and agreed to Grey’s conference proposal only afterward.
choices.after: Two days later Berchtold replied that not a single point of the ultimatum could be withdrawn and that its text could not be discussed. Germany, too, rejected Grey’s conference proposal on 27 July, and Vienna resolved to present Europe with a fait accompli before any mediation could begin.

choices.text: Accept Grey’s conference as it stands, and promise that Russia will halt even its military preparations while the conference sits
choices.why: Lay down the sword first, and Germany has no grounds left to refuse
choices.after: Grey warmly welcomed the offer, and Germany’s grounds for refusing the conference shrank accordingly. But Vienna resolved to declare war before any conference could meet.

choices.text: Announce in the official Gazette that Russia mobilizes the day Austrian troops cross, so Vienna stops counting on mere protests
choices.why: Only a public pledge will keep Vienna and Berlin from calling it a bluff
choices.after: The warning ran on the front pages and the demonstrators cheered. In Berlin, Moltke urged Austria to hurry, saying that Russia had made the first threat.

note.text: According to Sazonov’s memoirs, he asked Berchtold to allow Ambassador Szápáry to go over the text of the ultimatum with him informally and revise it, but after waiting 48 hours he received a refusal.

RU-04a.title: The Regent’s Appeal

telegram.text: Regent Alexander to Nicholas II / Some demands incompatible with dignity of an independent state / Time limit too short / Austro-Hungarian army concentrating on frontier, Serbia unable to defend itself / Beg Your Majesty to come to our aid as soon as possible

RU-04a.event: Serbia’s reply was drafted by Pašić and his ministers themselves in Belgrade. Some historians argue, however, that the reply grew firmer after Spalajković, the Serbian minister in St Petersburg, sent a series of telegrams reporting Russian support. Since 26 July the regulations on the period preparatory to war have been in force in Russia.
RU-04a.scene: The Regent’s telegram has been awaiting an answer for three days. The Regent wrote that Serbia would accept not only those demands compatible with the position of an independent state but also any that you advised it to accept. There is neither a political alliance nor a military convention between Russia and Serbia, but when Prime Minister Pašić visited you at Tsarskoe Selo in early February he asked for arms in the hope of Russian support, and the Pan-Slav newspapers write that Russia must not abandon a brother nation. Today you have heard reports from Navy Minister Grigorovich and Interior Minister Maklakov, and this evening Sazonov’s written report lies before you.

voices.text: Serbia has staked its fate on a single word from Your Majesty. The Regent has already said that Serbia will follow Russia’s wishes on what to accept and what to reject.

Serbia must not be made to feel abandoned, but any wording that promises military support would hand Vienna and Berlin a pretext. Urge Serbia to strive for peace, Your Majesty, and say only that Russia will not turn away from it.
There was little interesting news, but from Sazonov’s written report it appears that the Austrians are evidently disconcerted by the rumor of our preparations and are beginning to talk.

voices.who: Nicholas II (from a note reportedly sent to Sazonov that day)
voices.text: An idea has come to me. What if Russia, after consulting France and England and then Germany and Italy, proposed to Austria that the dispute with Serbia be referred to the tribunal at The Hague? Hope for peace is not yet lost.

choices.text: Reply as the 24 July Council resolved: no armed resistance, Serbia’s fate left to the Powers, and no promise of military aid
choices.why: Russia cannot bear the cost of a war fought for Serbia
choices.after: The reply stunned the Serbian government at Niš. Through Spalajković, Pašić asked whether Russia was telling Serbia to retreat again, as in 1909.

choices.text: Grant Spalajković’s plea: reply that Russia will defend Serbia with its army, and have the reply printed in the official Gazette
choices.why: Only a clear pledge can stop Vienna’s advance into Serbia
choices.after: Demonstrators marched through the capital waving newspapers that carried the reply. In Berlin the view spread that Russia had already decided to fight on Serbia’s side, and Vienna hurried its declaration of war.

choices.text: Urge Serbia to strive to the last to avoid bloodshed, but reply that Russia will in no case be indifferent to Serbia’s fate
choices.why: Promise nothing, but keep hold of Serbia’s trust and goodwill
choices.after: The reply left for Niš on 27 July: “So long as the slightest hope exists of avoiding bloodshed, all our efforts must be directed to that end; but if in spite of our earnest wish we are not successful, your Highness may rest assured that Russia will in no case disinterest herself in the fate of Serbia.” On 30 July the Regent sent a telegram of thanks saying that the future of Serbia was secure now that it was the object of your gracious solicitude. In the meantime, at noon on 28 July, Vienna had declared war on Serbia.

note.text: There was no treaty of alliance between Russia and Serbia. On 24 July the Council of Ministers decided to advise Serbia not to resist by force, and the Emperor’s reply did not promise military support either. But the words ‘will in no case disinterest herself’ led Serbia to expect Russia’s protection.

pressure.title: A Brother’s Appeal
pressure.text: As a young man Regent Alexander studied at an elite military school for the nobility in St Petersburg, and his mother was a Montenegrin princess, a sister of Grand Duchess Anastasia. When you received Pašić at Tsarskoe Selo in February 1914, Pašić reported home that you had said you would do everything for Serbia. Pan-Slav societies and newspapers demand that Russia not abandon a brother nation. If you reject the Regent’s appeal, the disappointment will be heard more loudly in St Petersburg than in Niš.

RU-05.title: War Is Declared

telegram.text: Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia / Notification sent by telegram

RU-05.scene: In the afternoon you and your daughters took tea with relatives at Strelna. Now, at 8:30 p.m., back at Peterhof, you receive Sazonov, who reports that Austria declared war on Serbia at noon today. Yanushkevich has prepared two draft decrees. One is a partial mobilization of only the four military districts of Kiev, Odessa, Moscow and Kazan; the other, a general mobilization of the whole empire. Sazonov believes that partial mobilization will send a signal aimed at Austria alone without provoking Germany, but Dobrorolsky, head of the General Staff’s mobilization section, and Quartermaster General Danilov protest that no such plan ever existed. Russia’s mobilization plan, revised in 1912, assumed war against Germany and Austria together, and a partial mobilization that left out the Warsaw military district could throw a later general mobilization into confusion.

voices.who: Dobrorolsky (head of the General Staff’s mobilization section)
voices.text: A plan for partial mobilization does not exist even on paper. The units in the southern districts depend on reservists and trains coming from other districts. Mobilize partially now, and the railway timetables will be tangled on the day a general mobilization becomes necessary.
A general mobilization will be read as a challenge to Germany. A partial mobilization aimed only at Austria would be hard for Berlin to object to, and Vienna would see that Russia is in earnest.

voices.who: Durnovo (former Interior Minister, memorandum to the Emperor, February 1914)
voices.text: In the event of defeat, the possibility of which in a struggle with a foe like Germany cannot be overlooked, social revolution in its most extreme form is inevitable.

choices.text: Seek a guarantee from the Powers for Vienna’s pledge not to annex Serbian territory, and put off mobilization until it is secured
choices.why: Save Serbia’s territory and Russia’s standing is saved too
choices.after: Nationalist newspapers attacked the government for repeating the ‘diplomatic Tsushima’ of 1909. Early the next morning came news that Austrian river monitors had begun shelling Belgrade.

choices.text: Approve Sazonov’s plan to mobilize four districts, to be announced on 29 July, and keep the general mobilization decree ready too
choices.why: Aim at Austria alone and a clash with Germany can be avoided
choices.after: Partial mobilization was announced on 29 July. At about 1 a.m. that day you sent Wilhelm a telegram in English from Peterhof: “An ignoble war has been declared to a weak country. … I beg you in the name of our old friendship to do what you can to stop your allies from going too far.”

choices.text: As Dobrorolsky and Danilov urge, skip partial mobilization and order general mobilization at once, German frontier included
choices.why: If Russia must fight Germany anyway, keep the railway timetables intact
choices.after: That night the work of collecting the ministers’ countersignatures on the decree began. With Poincaré still at sea, the Foreign Ministry in Paris drafted a telegram voicing concern at Russia’s haste.

note.text: In the Bosnian crisis of 1909, Russia yielded to a virtual German ultimatum and recognized Austria’s annexation of Bosnia. In Russia this was called a ‘diplomatic Tsushima’, after the disastrous defeat in the war with Japan.

RU-06.title: Two Decrees

map.caption: Belgrade, a frontier city where the Sava meets the Danube, was shelled early on 29 July by batteries across the river at Zemun and by Austrian river monitors.

RU-06.event: Early on 29 July, Austrian river monitors and batteries at Zemun, across the Sava, began shelling Belgrade. The same day the German ambassador Pourtalès conveyed a warning from Bethmann Hollweg to Sazonov: if Russia continued its military preparations, Germany would have no choice but to mobilize, and a European war could then scarcely be prevented. The Russian Foreign Ministry diary records this warning in the words that Germany would mobilize, ‘in which case she would immediately proceed to take the offensive’.
RU-06.scene: In the morning Yanushkevich arrives with two decrees, one for partial and one for general mobilization. The general mobilization decree needs the ministers’ countersignatures to take effect, so once you sign, Dobrorolsky will carry it around the capital. Your diary records the day like this: “The day was unusually troubled. I was constantly called to the telephone, now by Sazonov, now by Sukhomlinov or Yanushkevich. Besides, I was in urgent telegraphic correspondence with Wilhelm.”

voices.text: If Your Majesty signs both, either one can be sent across the country within an hour. The decision can wait until evening.

voices.who: Sazonov (to Ambassador Pourtalès, in the afternoon)
voices.text: Now I no longer have any doubt as to the true causes of Austria’s intransigence.

voices.who: Pourtalès (German ambassador, jumping up from his chair)
voices.text: I protest with all my strength, Minister, against this wounding assertion.

choices.text: Sign both of the decrees Yanushkevich has brought, and decide by evening, as events unfold, which one to send out
choices.why: Put off the decision, but keep either option ready for immediate use
choices.after: After Pourtalès’s warning and the news of the shelling of Belgrade had come in one after the other, Sazonov, Sukhomlinov and Yanushkevich met in the Chief of Staff’s office and recommended general mobilization, and you gave your consent by telephone. Dobrorolsky took the countersigned decree to the Central Telegraph Office, where the operators made ready to send it to every corner of the empire.

choices.text: Accept the General Staff’s view that partial mobilization will snarl the railways: sign the general decree and send it out today
choices.why: General mobilization is the only technically workable course
choices.after: Late in the afternoon Dobrorolsky obtained the ministers’ countersignatures and went to the Central Telegraph Office. The operators began sending the mobilization telegram to military districts across the empire.

choices.text: Sign only the partial decree, and tell Yanushkevich the general one stays in the drawer unless Germany mobilizes first
choices.why: At least avoid being the monarch who signed general mobilization first
choices.after: Yanushkevich bowed his head but did not give way. That night, in an exchange of telegrams with Wilhelm, you proposed referring the Austro-Serbian question to The Hague conference.

note.text: Belgrade lay right on the frontier where the Sava joins the Danube, within range of shells fired from Zemun on the Austrian bank opposite. That is why the Serbian government had moved to Niš before the war.

RU-06G.title: The Telegrams Go Out

telegram.text: Willy to Nicky / Cannot consider Austria’s action an ‘ignoble’ war / Quite possible for Russia to remain a spectator / Russian military measures would jeopardize my position as mediator

RU-06G.scene: Wilhelm’s telegram arrived when the general mobilization telegrams were already going out to the empire’s military districts. He says that Russia can remain a spectator of this conflict and offers to help direct talks with Vienna, yet warns that Russian military measures will ruin his mediation. Sukhomlinov says that stopping a mobilization once begun will wreck the entire railway timetable, while the Empress begs you to trust Wilhelm’s word just once more.

voices.text: Your Majesty, mobilization means thousands of trains meshing together at fixed times. Stop it now, and the reservists will be stranded at the stations and the horses in the wagons. Starting again would take days.
Germany is only playing for time. Wilhelm’s telegram and Pourtalès’s communication say entirely different things.

choices.text: Take Sukhomlinov’s point that a mobilization once begun cannot be halted: let it run, and tell Wilhelm it does not mean war
choices.why: Halt now and the whole railway timetable collapses
choices.after: Berlin learned of Russia’s general mobilization more than a day earlier than it did in the actual crisis. Moltke pressed the Kaiser hard, saying there was no reason to wait any longer.

choices.text: Yield to the Empress: halt general mobilization, revert to partial mobilization, and pin your hopes again on Wilhelm’s mediation
choices.why: Save the chance of mediation, even at the cost of confusion
choices.after: Cancellation orders followed to the districts that had already received the telegram, and the General Staff was thrown into confusion. Yanushkevich said he would telephone again the next morning.

note.text: Mobilization in 1914 was a single plan in which thousands of railway timetables meshed together, so halting it midway or changing its direction caused great confusion. One example is the confusion Austria-Hungary suffered in early August, when it diverted its Second Army, bound for Serbia, to Galicia.

RU-07.place: Peterhof / Central Telegraph Office, St Petersburg
RU-07.title: Willy’s Telegram

telegram.text: Willy to Nicky / Cannot consider Austria’s action an ‘ignoble’ war / Quite possible for Russia to remain a spectator / Russian military measures would jeopardize my position as mediator

RU-07.scene: At 8:20 p.m. you had already sent Wilhelm a telegram proposing that the Austro-Serbian problem be given over to The Hague conference. At the Central Telegraph Office in St Petersburg, Dobrorolsky stands holding the countersigned general mobilization decree, and the operators are ready to send it to military districts across the empire. Then Wilhelm’s reply comes in. He says that Russia can remain a spectator of the conflict, and warns that Russian military measures would jeopardize his position as mediator. A single word into the telephone would stop the decree; leave it, and millions of men will begin to move tonight.

voices.text: I think a direct understanding between your Government and Vienna possible and desirable … Of course, military measures on the part of Russia which could be looked upon by Austria as threatening would precipitate a calamity we both wish to avoid, and jeopardize my position as mediator which I readily accepted on your appeal to my friendship and my help.
The decree is already at the telegraph office. Stop it once and it will take a day to set it going again, and that day puts Warsaw in danger.

voices.who: Nicholas II (to those around him, as reported)
voices.text: I will not be responsible for a monstrous slaughter. Everything that might preserve the peace must be done.

choices.text: Halt all mobilization, publish your Hague proposal to Wilhelm in a government communiqué, and await word from Vienna and Berlin
choices.why: With the whole world watching, even Germany will find mediation hard to refuse
choices.after: When the government communiqué announced the proposal for arbitration at The Hague, the newspapers of Europe were abuzz. The General Staff and the Pan-Slav press were furious that the Emperor had abandoned Serbia.

choices.text: As Yanushkevich urges, send the general mobilization telegrams as planned, and tell Wilhelm that mobilization does not mean war
choices.why: Lose a single day and Warsaw is in danger
choices.after: That night the general mobilization telegrams went out to every military district. Berlin confirmed the news the next morning, and Moltke declared there was no reason to wait any longer.

choices.text: By telephone, cancel general mobilization, order partial mobilization of four southern districts only, and rely on Wilhelm
choices.why: Better a day’s loss than responsibility for a slaughter
choices.after: At about 9:30 p.m. (about 11 p.m., by some accounts) the cancellation order was passed on, and Dobrorolsky withdrew the decree. The partial mobilization telegrams for the four southern districts went out instead. At 1:20 a.m. on the 30th you telegraphed Wilhelm again, explaining that ‘the military measures which have now come into force were decided five days ago’.

note.text: The First Hague Peace Conference of 1899 was convened at Nicholas II’s proposal. The collection of documents the German government published in 1914 left out the 29 July telegram proposing reference to The Hague, which became known only when Russia published it in January 1915.

RU-08.title: “I Will Decide”

telegram.text: Willy to Nicky / If Russia mobilizes against Austria, my role as mediator will be endangered if not ruined / Whole weight of decision lies solely on your shoulders now / You bear responsibility for peace or war

RU-08.event: At about 11 a.m. Sukhomlinov and Yanushkevich again asked you by telephone for general mobilization, but you flatly refused and tried to end the call. When Yanushkevich said that Sazonov was with him, you were silent for some time and then answered that you would see Sazonov at 3 p.m. That day the Berlin newspaper Lokal-Anzeiger put out a special edition announcing German general mobilization, then promptly denied it.
RU-08.scene: Sazonov met Krivoshein over lunch in a private room at Donon’s restaurant and then came on to Peterhof. Tired and anxious, you have General Tatishchev, who leaves for Berlin today, sit in on the audience. From 3:10 to 4 p.m. Sazonov explains that Germany has rejected every proposal for mediation and that German mobilization has advanced considerably without any official announcement. Handing him Wilhelm’s telegram, you say: “He is asking the impossible. … If I agreed to Germany’s demands now, we should find ourselves unarmed against the Austrian Army which is mobilized already. It would be madness.” Then, after a long silence, you add: “This would mean sending hundreds of thousands of Russian people to their death. How can one help hesitating to take such a step?”

voices.text: After that I shall go away, smash my telephone and generally adopt measures which will prevent anyone from finding me for the purpose of giving contrary orders which would again stop our general mobilization.
Otherwise we should be marching towards a certain catastrophe.
Yes, it is hard to decide.

choices.text: Halt all mobilization, and stake your last hope on the compromise formula Sazonov gave Pourtalès and on referral to The Hague
choices.why: Disarm first, and Berlin will be free to press Vienna
choices.after: The General Staff was aghast at the order to halt mobilization, and Sukhomlinov came with his resignation. In Berlin, Bethmann Hollweg began pressing Vienna to seize the opening.

choices.text: Accept Sazonov’s report that German mobilization is well advanced, and have the general mobilization decree sent out again
choices.why: Delay arming and Russia stands defenseless before two enemies
choices.after: When Tatishchev spoke, you cut him off roughly with “I will decide”, and at last gave your consent to general mobilization. Sazonov went downstairs to the palace telephone to pass the order to Yanushkevich, adding: “Now you can smash your telephone.” The next morning general mobilization notices were posted in every street of the capital.

choices.text: Keep to partial mobilization, and give Tatishchev, leaving for Berlin today, instructions to persuade Wilhelm in person
choices.why: The direct channel between the two emperors is not yet closed
choices.after: Sazonov left the study pale, and Yanushkevich reported again that the mobilization plan was falling apart. Paléologue telegraphed Paris that Russia was wavering.

note.text: On 30 July Sazonov gave Pourtalès a formula: ‘if Austria … declares herself ready to eliminate from her ultimatum those items which violate the principle of Serbian sovereignty, Russia undertakes to cease all her military preparations’. Jagow, State Secretary at the German Foreign Office, at once rejected it as unacceptable to Austria.

pressure.title: Hundreds of Thousands of Deaths
pressure.text: You are the monarch who proposed the Hague Peace Conference of 1899. The thought that signing the general mobilization decree will send hundreds of thousands of men to their deaths holds you back, and today you said as much to Sazonov. Rasputin, on his sickbed in Tyumen, is also said to have sent a telegram begging you to prevent war. The generals, on the other hand, say that every day of delay puts Warsaw in greater danger.

RU-09.title: Twelve Hours
RU-09.clock: About 12 hours until Germany’s deadline (noon, 1 August)

telegram.text: Willy to Nicky / Authentic news of serious preparations for war on my eastern frontier / Safety of my empire forces preventive defensive measures upon me / Peace of Europe may still be maintained by you if Russia will agree to stop military measures which must threaten Germany and Austria-Hungary

RU-09.event: On the morning of 31 July general mobilization notices went up in every street of the capital. The same day Austria-Hungary ordered general mobilization, and Germany proclaimed a ‘state of imminent danger of war’. In the afternoon at Peterhof you received Pourtalès and told him that the Russian army would not provoke anyone while mediation continued.
RU-09.scene: Late at night (11 p.m. by Paléologue’s account, midnight by Sazonov’s recollection) the German ambassador Pourtalès comes to the Foreign Ministry and informs Sazonov that unless Russia halts its mobilization within 12 hours on both the German and the Austrian frontiers, the whole German army will be mobilized. The deadline is noon tomorrow. Sazonov replies that Russia will not attack as long as negotiations continue, but that demobilizing without wrecking the entire military organization is technically impossible. The report goes up to you at Peterhof.

voices.text: If mobilization stops, thousands of trains will halt on the line and the reservists will spend the night at the stations instead of in barracks. Starting again would take weeks, and by then the whole German army will be massed at the frontier.
France will fulfill the obligations of the alliance. If Russia backs down at this moment, France will face the entire German army alone.

choices.text: Refuse Germany’s demand and continue mobilizing, but repeat to Wilhelm your promise not to attack while negotiations go on
choices.why: Halting mobilization now would be as good as disarming
choices.after: You had already telegraphed Wilhelm that afternoon: “As long as the negotiations with Austria on Serbia’s account are taking place my troops shall not make any provocative action. I give you my solemn word for this.” The noon deadline of 1 August passed without Russia meeting the demand, and at 5 p.m. that day Germany ordered general mobilization.

choices.text: Heed Rasputin’s telegram that war will doom Russia and the dynasty: cancel all mobilization and leave Serbia to the Powers
choices.why: The dynasty and the country come first, even at the cost of prestige
choices.after: When the decree was revoked, the crowds gathered before the Winter Palace dispersed in silence. In Paris, a stunned Poincaré declared that the alliance had collapsed.

choices.text: Seize on Jagow’s word that Germany will not mobilize if Russia mobilizes only in the south: offer to halt on the German frontier
choices.why: Keep the contest with Austria, but avoid war with Germany
choices.after: Pourtalès telegraphed Berlin with visible relief. But Moltke regarded the Russian troops on the Austrian frontier as a threat to Germany too, and would not set his suspicions aside.

note.text: Germany gave Russia 12 hours and France 18. The instructions for France also demanded that, if France chose neutrality, it hand over the fortresses of Toul and Verdun as a pledge, but since France did not declare neutrality, the demand was never actually presented.

RU-10.title: Pourtalès in Tears
RU-10.event: On the afternoon of 1 August you sent Wilhelm a last telegram. You understood that he was obliged to mobilize, it said, but you wished to have from him the same guarantee you had given him, that these measures did not mean war. Wilhelm replied that since no answer had come by noon, Germany too had been obliged to mobilize.
RU-10.scene: At 7 p.m. Pourtalès comes to the Foreign Ministry and asks three times whether Russia is prepared to give a favorable answer to the ultimatum. When Sazonov gives the same answer all three times, the ambassador hands over the declaration of war with a shaking hand, then leans against the window and bursts into tears; the two men embrace and part. At that hour you are at the evening service, and only on your return do you hear that Germany has declared war. You wanted to lead the army yourself, but the ministers dissuaded you, saying that the Emperor must not leave the capital. The name put forward for the post is that of your father’s cousin, Grand Duke Nicholas Nikolaevich.

voices.text: Who could have thought that I should be leaving St. Petersburg under such circumstances!
If Your Majesty commands the army in person, every defeat at the front becomes the Emperor’s defeat. Your Majesty must remain in the capital and lead the whole country.
The army awaits Your Majesty’s orders. Whoever is to command, Your Majesty must decide as soon as possible.

choices.text: Override the ministers and take supreme command yourself, trusting that troops fight to the end only with the Emperor beside them
choices.why: Only if the Emperor leads in person will army and people stand as one
choices.after: The ministers objected that the government would falter if the Emperor left the capital, but you would not be moved. It was in September 1915, as the Great Retreat was drawing to a close, that you actually took this decision.

choices.text: Appoint Grand Duke Nicholas Nikolaevich Supreme Commander and, as the ministers advise, remain in the capital to lead the country
choices.why: A defeat at the front must not become the Emperor’s own defeat
choices.after: After lunch that day you summoned the Grand Duke and told him he was appointed Supreme Commander. Nearly two meters tall, the Grand Duke was popular in the army. In your diary you noted that the appointment was ‘until my arrival at the army’, and in September 1915 you did in the end take supreme command yourself. That night the British ambassador Buchanan brought a telegram from George V, and you spent a long time with him drafting the reply.

note.text: The declaration of war that Pourtalès handed over contained two alternative passages, one stating that ‘Russia has not replied’ and the other that ‘Russia’s reply is unsatisfactory’. The mistake arose when the German embassy copied the two versions it had received from Berlin into a single text.

RU-11.title: Save the West from the East

map.caption: Russia sent two armies into East Prussia and four into Galicia. At the end of August the Second Army collapsed at Tannenberg; in early September Russian troops took Lemberg.

RU-11.event: On 2 August, in the Nicholas Hall of the Winter Palace, you had the manifesto declaring war read aloud, then, before the altar, raised your right hand toward the Gospels and repeated the oath Alexander I had sworn in 1812. The crowd filling Palace Square saw you on the balcony, fell to its knees as one and sang the national anthem. On 3 August Germany declared war on France, and on 4 August, when German troops entered Belgium, Britain entered the war.
RU-11.scene: While the main German force advances through Belgium into France, Paris wants Russia to invade East Prussia as soon as possible and draw German troops eastward. In staff talks between the two countries in 1912 and 1913, Russia promised to attack Germany with 800,000 men once the 15th day of mobilization had passed. But the strategic railways are unfinished, trains must stop at the frontier because of the different gauge, and many units must set off without their full complement of reservists, horses and transport wagons. Stavka has proposed sending Rennenkampf’s First Army and Samsonov’s Second Army into East Prussia, and four armies into Galicia.

voices.who: Nicholas II (to the officers of the Guard, Winter Palace, 2 August)
voices.text: I solemnly swear that I will never make peace so long as one of the enemy is on the soil of the fatherland.
The French army is taking the full weight of the main German offensive. Bring forward the East Prussian offensive by even a single day. That is the way to save the alliance.
Russia’s chief enemy is Austria. Only by crushing the Austrian army in Galicia first can Russia save its Slav brothers in the Balkans too. Divide the army’s strength in two and it will win nowhere.

choices.text: As Alexeyev argues, stand on the defensive in East Prussia and throw everything into Galicia to crush the Austrian army first
choices.why: Divide your strength in two and you win on neither front
choices.after: The victory in Galicia might have been larger and faster. But with the East quiet, Germany did not withdraw a single soldier from the west, and Paris was furious that Russia had broken its promise.

choices.text: As Danilov urged in his 1910 plan, concentrate on East Prussia and put the promise to draw German troops eastward first
choices.why: If the alliance collapses, Russia cannot hold out alone either
choices.after: More troops went into East Prussia, but the railways and supply lines could not sustain them. The Austrian army in Galicia, meanwhile, pushed deep into Russian Poland.

choices.text: As Stavka proposes, rush two armies into East Prussia, and strike the Austrians in Galicia with the main force of four armies
choices.why: Keep the promise to France and serve Russia’s own interests too
choices.after: The First Army crossed the East Prussian frontier on 17 August and won at Gumbinnen on the 20th, but on 26–30 August the Second Army was encircled and destroyed at Tannenberg, and Samsonov took his own life. In Galicia, Russian forces drove the Austrians back from 23 August and took Lemberg (Lviv) in early September. Germany withdrew two army corps from the west and sent them east; historians debate how much this affected the Battle of the Marne.

note.text: Russian railways used a wider gauge (about 1,524 mm) than those of Western Europe. Because the Russian lines stopped at the frontier, the Russian troops who entered East Prussia had to rely on horses and carts for supply.

RU-12.title: Petrograd

telegram.text: Second Army in southern East Prussia / Germans attacked 13th and 15th Corps with overwhelming forces / Both corps almost annihilated by heavy artillery fire / General Samsonov killed

RU-12.event: In late August, around Tannenberg in southern East Prussia, Samsonov’s Second Army was encircled by the German Eighth Army. The Grand Duke, as Supreme Commander, ordered the news withheld for several days, and only on 2 September did the General Staff announce briefly that two corps had suffered heavy losses and that General Samsonov had been killed. Meanwhile, in Galicia, Russian troops are driving the Austrians back and closing in on Lemberg.
RU-12.scene: On 30 August Sazonov told Ambassador Paléologue that Samsonov’s army had been destroyed, and the next day the grave news reached you too. In France the Germans are nearing Paris, and St Petersburg worries whether its ally can hold. Since the outbreak of war, anti-German feeling has run high in the capital: on 4 August a mob sacked the German embassy on St Isaac’s Square, and shops and people with German names have fallen under suspicion. Amid all this, there is talk of replacing the German-style name ‘Sankt-Peterburg’ with a Russian one.

voices.text: Received grave news from the 2nd Army: the Germans fell upon the 13th and 15th Corps with overwhelming forces and almost annihilated them with heavy artillery fire. Gen. Samsonov and many others have perished!

voices.who: Sazonov (to Paléologue on 30 August, as Paléologue recalled it)
voices.text: Samsonov’s army has been destroyed. Russia owed this sacrifice to France, since France has shown herself a perfect ally.

As a protest of Slav nationalism against Germany, the new name is emphatic enough, but to give a Slav name to a capital that Peter the Great built as a modern, Western city is a contradiction of history.

choices.text: Sign the decree renaming the capital Petrograd, and keep up the measures banning the sale of vodka for the duration of the war
choices.why: In wartime the government must have national feeling on its side
choices.after: The decree was signed on the evening of 31 August, and the capital became Petrograd. On 3 September, when news came of the capture of Lemberg and Halych, you wrote in your diary that you were overjoyed. On 4 September an order banned the sale of alcohol for the duration of the war, and that evening you saw Rasputin for the first time since he was stabbed.

choices.text: Order an inquiry into Zhilinsky, commander of the Northwestern Front, over Tannenberg, and say you will go to Stavka in person
choices.why: Military discipline requires clear responsibility for defeat
choices.after: The Grand Duke resented the Emperor’s meddling in command at the front, and the ministers once again urged you not to leave the capital. Among the generals, recriminations flew over who should bear the blame for the defeat.

choices.text: Keep the name, and order Interior Minister Maklakov to crack down on looting and riots against subjects of German descent
choices.why: Russia cannot afford to lose its officers and officials of German descent
choices.after: The Baltic German nobles and officers were relieved, but nationalist newspapers whispered that the court was shielding Germans. Suspicion of the German-born Empress grew accordingly.

note.text: ‘Sankt-Peterburg’, meaning ‘city of St Peter’, was a Dutch-German style of name, while ‘Petrograd’, meaning ‘Peter’s city’, is a Russian form. The city was renamed Leningrad in 1924 and became St Petersburg again in 1991.

pressure.title: A German Name
pressure.text: The Empress comes from the grand ducal house of Hesse in Germany, and many high posts at court and in the army are held by German nobles from the Baltic provinces. On 4 August the crowd in the capital sacked the German embassy on St Isaac’s Square. Your mother, Maria Feodorovna, returning from England, was refused passage across the frontier at Berlin and had to go around by way of Denmark and Sweden, reaching Peterhof only on 9 August. If the court gives the impression of shielding anything connected with Germany, suspicion will turn straight to the imperial family.

RU-13.title: The Straits and Romania

map.caption: A large share of Russia’s exports passed through the Straits linking the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Romania and Bulgaria stayed neutral in the autumn of 1914.

telegram.text: German battlecruiser Goeben and light cruiser Breslau enter Dardanelles / Ottoman government permits passage / British squadron’s pursuit fails

RU-13.event: On 2 August the Ottoman Empire concluded a secret alliance with Germany while still professing neutrality. From 5 August, War Minister Enver instead proposed an alliance with Russia to the Russian military attaché Leontiev, asking in return for Western Thrace and the Aegean islands. Sazonov did not trust the offer but ordered the talks kept going to gain time. On 10 August the Goeben and Breslau entered the Straits, the Ottoman government announced that it had bought the two ships from Germany, and at the end of September the Straits were closed to foreign shipping.
RU-13.scene: Sazonov has submitted the text of an agreement to be exchanged with Romania. Romania decided on neutrality at a crown council in early August, and Prime Minister Brătianu has said that Romania will remain neutral to the end if it is guaranteed, after the war, the lands of Austria-Hungary where Romanians are the majority. Under the agreement Russia recognizes that right, and in return Romania observes a neutrality benevolent to Russia; Russia takes this ‘benevolent neutrality’ to include help in getting supplies through to Serbia. Bulgaria too has declared neutrality, but although Sazonov has pressed Serbia since early August to promise part of Macedonia to Bulgaria, Pašić has evaded the demand by attaching conditions. The Black Sea Fleet waits for the day the Goeben comes out into the Black Sea.

voices.text: If Romania stays neutral, Austria must worry about its eastern flank, and the road to Serbia opens. If the Ottomans pick a fight, they must be the ones to fire first if London and Paris are to stand with Russia.

voices.who: Admiral Eberhard (commander of the Black Sea Fleet)
voices.text: Your Majesty, the Goeben alone is faster and stronger than any battleship in the Black Sea Fleet. She must be stopped off the Bosporus before she comes out into the Black Sea.

choices.text: Put off the deal with Romania to bring in Bulgaria first, and press Pašić harder to give up part of Macedonia
choices.why: If Bulgaria moves, the Ottomans will not dare to act rashly
choices.after: Pašić held out, saying that only the Serbian parliament could cede territory, and the Russian pressure left only deep distrust in Niš. Bulgaria stayed neutral, weighing the prices both sides offered, and in October 1915 it finally joined Germany and Austria and attacked Serbia.

choices.text: Approve the agreement buying Romania’s benevolent neutrality, and leave the Black Sea Fleet’s order not to fire first in place
choices.why: The Ottomans must fire first if Britain and France are to follow
choices.realNote: According to the Foreign Ministry diary, the Emperor received Sazonov’s report before the texts were exchanged and approved the signature. It is true that the Black Sea Fleet was ordered not to fire first, but it is not confirmed that the Emperor gave that order himself.
choices.after: The texts were exchanged around 1 October, and Romania remained neutral until August 1916. Early on 29 October the Ottoman fleet under the German admiral Souchon raided Odessa and Sevastopol, and on 2 November Russia declared war on the Ottoman Empire. In March and April 1915 Britain and France promised to give Constantinople and the Straits to Russia in the event of victory.

choices.text: Grant Admiral Eberhard’s request: send the Black Sea Fleet off the Bosporus to stop the Goeben before she reaches the Black Sea
choices.why: Wait for the enemy to fire, and Russia loses the sea first
choices.after: When the fleet left Sevastopol, the German officers in Constantinople were glad of it. News that Russia had moved first badly weakened the neutralists in the Ottoman government.

note.text: Russia was Serbia’s chief patron, but it could not steer Serbia at will. On 4 September, answering the Allies’ joint note, Pašić accepted the principle of a Macedonian concession, but attached conditions such as Bulgaria’s entry into the war and Serbian access to the Adriatic, and insisted that only parliament could decide on ceding territory.

BS-01.place: Black Sea, off the Bosporus / Petrograd
BS-01.title: Off the Bosporus
BS-01.scene: The battleships of the Black Sea Fleet have laid mines and begun patrolling off the mouth of the Bosporus. The Goeben stayed inside the Straits, but Enver and the German officers stirred up the newspapers, saying Russia had blockaded the Ottoman sea, and the standing of the Grand Vizier, Said Halim, who wanted neutrality, was badly weakened. In London, Grey is displeased that Russia moved first and worries about unrest among the Muslims of British India. Sazonov says that, now that things have come to this, Russia should make the Straits themselves a war aim.

voices.text: It was only a matter of time before the Ottomans sided with Germany. Russia must now secure promises from Britain and France that Constantinople and the Straits will go to Russia.
Your Majesty, there are no troops to send to Constantinople. Not a single corps can be spared from the fronts facing Germany and Austria.

choices.text: Make the Straits a war aim, prepare a landing, and press Britain and France to recognize Russia’s claim to Constantinople
choices.why: If Russia must fight, it should win its old goal, the Straits
choices.after: Britain and France reluctantly agreed to negotiate, but Russian troops for a landing were never found. Contrary to Russia’s hopes, the struggle for the Straits passed into British and French hands.

choices.text: With no troops to spare, pull the fleet back to Sevastopol and seek Ottoman neutrality by guaranteeing its territory
choices.why: Russia cannot afford to open yet another front
choices.after: The neutralists in the Ottoman government breathed again, but German gold and officers were already in Constantinople. The Ottoman entry into the war was delayed by only a few weeks.

note.text: In the autumn of 1914 the Russian Black Sea Fleet had not a single dreadnought. The first Russian dreadnought in the Black Sea, the Imperatritsa Mariya, did not enter service until 1915.

RS-01.title: The Fear of Abandonment
RS-01.scene: As soon as the Council of Ministers has decided to advise Serbia to give way, the Serbian minister, Miroslav Spalajković, hurries to the Foreign Ministry. Ever since Sarajevo he has been telling the Russian newspapers that Serbia bears no responsibility. Since Hartwig, the Russian minister in Belgrade, collapsed and died two weeks ago while calling at the Austrian legation, many in Serbia believe that Austria poisoned him. Spalajković pleads that if Russia abandons Serbia, every Slav in the Balkans will turn against Russia, and Sazonov, noting that the deadline is 6 p.m. tomorrow, asks for your decision.

voices.text: In 1909 Serbia listened to Russia and backed down. If it backs down again, Serbia will become an Austrian protectorate, and Russia will lose its last friend in the Balkans.
Even rejecting point 6 alone will give Vienna its pretext. Only if Serbia accepts everything will the pretext vanish, and then all Europe will see that Vienna is in the wrong.

choices.text: Accept Sazonov’s view that Vienna’s pretext must go: advise Belgrade to accept the whole ultimatum, point 6 included
choices.why: Remove the pretext and all Europe will see that Vienna is at fault
choices.after: Pašić, who had been away campaigning for the election, returned to Belgrade and spent the night revising the text with his ministers. Regent Alexander concluded that, with Russia advising it, Serbia had no other choice.

choices.text: Advise accepting most demands but referring the point 6 inquiry to The Hague tribunal or the Powers party to the 1909 declaration
choices.why: Keep sovereignty intact and leave the judgment to the Powers
choices.after: Instead of rejecting point 6, Serbia’s reply proposed another path, an international inquiry, and so went a step further than the reply Serbia actually sent.

note.text: On 10 July 1914 Hartwig called on Giesl, the Austrian minister in Belgrade, and died of a heart attack. Serbian newspapers at once ran stories claiming that Austria had poisoned him.

RS-02.title: Vienna Loses Its Pretext
RS-02.event: Just before the deadline, Serbia’s reply was delivered to the Austrian legation. As Russia had advised, Serbia accepted almost all the demands.
RS-02.scene: Even after reading the reply, Minister Giesl could not pack his bags at once. But in mid-July Vienna’s leaders had told the German ambassador Tschirschky that the ultimatum would be drafted so that Serbia was hardly likely to accept it. Conrad, Chief of the General Staff, insists that Serbia must be attacked regardless, while Wilhelm in Berlin would doubtless say that every cause for war had now vanished. Vienna’s next move depends on what Russia does.

voices.text: Before the world, the fault now lies with Vienna. If a conference of the Powers in London supervises Serbia’s compliance, Austria will have nowhere further to go.
Guarantees on paper alone cannot stop Austria. Only troops posted on the frontier will make Vienna listen to Russia.

choices.text: Propose an ambassadors’ conference to Grey first, so the Powers supervise Serbia’s compliance, and pledge Russia to abide by it
choices.why: Under Europe’s supervision, Vienna has no grounds to go further
choices.after: Grey replied that he would convene the conference at once, and France and Italy agreed. Germany hesitated, saying it could not haul its ally before a ‘European court’.

choices.text: As the Grand Duke urges, warn Vienna that attacking a Serbia that has yielded means mobilizing four southern districts
choices.why: Paper guarantees alone will never stop Austria
choices.after: The warning only provoked Vienna’s hard-liners. Conrad insisted that Austria must hurry before Russia could intervene.

choices.text: Do not move first now that Serbia has removed the pretext: wait for Berlin and London to restrain Vienna
choices.why: Acting rashly would only hand Vienna a fresh pretext
choices.after: When Russia said nothing, Vienna took it to mean that Russia would back down once again. Berchtold ordered his officials to find flaws in Serbia’s reply.

note.text: In fact, when Wilhelm II first read Serbia’s reply on 28 July, he wrote in the margin that with it ‘every cause for war’ had vanished. Had the reply accepted point 6 as well, Vienna’s case would have been weaker still.

RS-03.title: A Second 1909?
RS-03.scene: As word spreads that Russia has advised Serbia to give way, the Pan-Slav newspapers write that the humiliation of 1909 has been repeated. Among nationalist Duma deputies and officers of the Guard there is talk that the Emperor has sold out his Slav brothers, and Krivoshein warns that the government is losing public support. On the other side, the conservative elder statesman Durnovo says that, as he warned in his February memorandum, war is the very road to revolution. Rasputin, recovering in hospital in Tyumen after being stabbed at his home village of Pokrovskoye on 12 July, has also sent the imperial family a telegram begging them to prevent war.

voices.text: Each time the government has retreated, Russia’s prestige has fallen. The people will not understand this decision, and in the end their discontent will turn on Your Majesty.
The defeated army, having lost its most dependable men, and carried away by the tide of primitive peasant desire for land, will find itself too demoralized to serve as a bulwark of law and order.

voices.who: Rasputin (telegram from his hospital bed in Tyumen)
voices.text: Do not make war. If war comes, it will be the end of Russia and of the imperial family. (The wording of his telegrams and letters varies from one account to another.)

choices.text: Accept Krivoshein’s warning: promise the Duma and the army to speed up the Great Programme and raise the defense budget sharply
choices.why: Pay for the retreat with armaments and win back public opinion
choices.after: The Duma responded with applause, and in Berlin Moltke, told that Russia’s rearmament could be complete before 1917, grew still more anxious.

choices.text: Citing Durnovo’s warning, explain publicly why you kept the peace, and use censorship to silence the newspapers calling for war
choices.why: Defeat and revolution are far more dangerous than humiliation
choices.after: Several newspapers were suspended, and it was rumored that the Emperor had been denounced in the Guard officers’ mess. The factory districts, on the other hand, began to grow quiet.

note.text: On 12 July (29 June Old Style) Rasputin was stabbed in the stomach by a woman named Khioniya Guseva at his home village of Pokrovskoye, and for some time hovered between life and death. The wording of the telegrams and letters he sent urging that war be prevented differs slightly from one account to another.

RS-03D.title: Durnovo’s Audience
RS-03D.scene: As you prepare to explain to the nation your decision to keep the peace, Pyotr Durnovo, a member of the State Council, asks for an audience. As Interior Minister in 1905–1906 he crushed the revolution, and in his February 1914 memorandum he warned that if Russia were drawn into the rivalry between Britain and Germany, defeat and revolution could follow. Durnovo urges you to use this moment to talk directly with Berlin and settle each side’s share in the Balkans, while Krivoshein counters that this would shake the alliance with France and make the Duma and public opinion even more suspicious of the government. The capital’s newspapers are already writing that the government has abandoned Serbia.

voices.text: Your Majesty, Germany and Russia have nothing to gain by fighting each other. If Russia bleeds for the rivalry between Britain and Germany, the only winners in the end will be the revolutionaries.
Make a separate bargain with Berlin and Paris will no longer trust Russia, and the people will think the government has given in to German pressure.

choices.text: As Durnovo advises, send Wilhelm a private telegram: if Vienna leaves Serbia’s territory alone, Russia will not move either
choices.why: A direct bargain between monarchs could settle the Balkans without war
choices.after: Wilhelm replied warmly that he would urge restraint on Vienna. But Ambassador Paléologue reported rumors to Paris that Russia was talking to Berlin behind its ally’s back.

choices.text: Heed Krivoshein’s warning against separate deals with Berlin, and assure Paléologue that the alliance with France stands firm
choices.why: Keep the peace, but do not lose the alliance in doing so
choices.after: Durnovo bowed and withdrew. Paléologue passed on to Paris the Emperor’s assurance that, although Russia had stepped back over Serbia, the alliance stood unchanged.

note.text: Durnovo’s memorandum held that Russia had nothing to gain from a war with Germany and that defeat would make an extreme social revolution inevitable. There is no confirmed record that Nicholas II actually read it.

RS-04.title: A Pledge Seized

map.caption: Belgrade was a frontier city facing Zemun across the Sava, and the Serbian government moved to Niš on 25 July.

RS-04.event: Instead of declaring war, Austria informed the Powers that it would occupy Belgrade as a pledge until Serbia kept its promises. The move follows the ‘Halt in Belgrade’ idea that Wilhelm II actually conceived on 28 July.
RS-04.scene: Austrian batteries have taken up position at Zemun across the Sava, and the Serbian army has already withdrawn inland. In London Grey is hurrying preparations for a conference, and Poincaré, soon to be home, asks how far Russia means to give way. The General Staff says the southern districts must be mobilized the moment Austrian troops cross the frontier, while Sazonov says that a guarantee that the occupation will be temporary is enough.

voices.text: If the southern districts do not move the day Austrian troops enter Belgrade, Vienna will believe that Russia will do nothing.
If the occupation is temporary and Serbia’s territory and sovereignty are guaranteed, handing over one capital as a pledge is a cheaper price than war.

choices.text: Accept, as Sazonov advises, a temporary occupation of Belgrade under the Powers’ supervision, with a fixed date for withdrawal
choices.why: Giving up one capital as a pledge costs less than a war
choices.after: Austrian troops entered Belgrade in early August and advanced no further. The Serbs were furious that Russia had given away their capital.

choices.text: As Yanushkevich urges, reject the occupation and warn that four southern districts will mobilize if Austrian troops cross
choices.why: Stand still, and Vienna will push on to the very end
choices.after: On receiving the warning, Vienna briefly halted its order to advance and asked Berlin’s view. But Moltke took Russia’s threat to mobilize as a threat to Germany.

choices.text: Have Serbia hand Tankosić and Ciganović, named in the ultimatum, to an international inquiry, and demand an end to the occupation
choices.why: Hand over the culprits and the occupation loses its justification
choices.after: Pašić agreed to hand over Major Tankosić and Ciganović, both named in the ultimatum. When the names of the Black Hand and Apis began to appear in the inquiry’s papers, the Serbian army grew restive.

note.text: The ‘Halt in Belgrade’ was a plan for Austria to occupy only the Serbian capital and hold it as a pledge while negotiating. Wilhelm II and Britain’s Grey came up with it separately at almost the same time, on 28–29 July.

RS-05.title: The Table in London
RS-05.scene: The ambassadors of Britain, Germany, France and Italy have gathered in a conference room at the Foreign Office in London, and the Russian and Austrian ambassadors attend to state their views. The issues are who will supervise the inquiry inside Serbia and, if Austrian troops are there, when they will leave. Sazonov says Russia should use the occasion to gain something else as well. At a special conference in February 1914, Russia had studied how to seize the Bosporus if a major war broke out, and the question of the Straits, through which the Black Sea trade passes, had always been a central concern of Russian diplomacy.

voices.text: If Russia gives ground on Serbia, it must in return have Germany and Austria recognize Russia’s interests in the Straits.
If Russia makes bargains at the conference without consulting its ally, Paris will ask what the alliance is for.

choices.text: Back mediation under which an international commission oversees the inquiry in Serbia and Austrian troops leave by a fixed date
choices.why: The crisis ends only if Serbia keeps its sovereignty and Vienna saves face
choices.after: The conference agreed on sending a commission and on a withdrawal date. In Vienna, Conrad resigned, calling it ‘yet another diplomatic defeat’.

choices.text: As Sazonov says, step back over Serbia, and in return win German and Austrian recognition of Russia’s interests in the Straits
choices.why: If Russia must concede, it should be paid well for it
choices.after: Germany offered vague promises about the Straits, and Britain and France were displeased that Russia had made a deal behind their backs.

choices.text: Backed by Pan-Slav opinion, demand the immediate withdrawal of Austrian troops, and walk out of the conference if refused
choices.why: Retreat again and the government cannot survive at home
choices.after: The conference came close to breaking down, and tension on the frontier did not ease all autumn.
