note.text: The ambassadors’ conference held in London from December 1912 to August 1913 dealt with the aftermath of the Balkan Wars, settling Albanian independence among other matters, and prevented war among the Great Powers.

RS-06.title: Toward the Next Crisis
RS-06.scene: Autumn has come without war, the Alexander Palace has returned to its usual routine, and Alexei turned ten in August. But the army and the Pan-Slavs say Russia must not back down in the next crisis, and France demands that Russia hurry the strategic railways to the western frontier in return for further loans. Conservatives such as Durnovo say instead that the old monarchical solidarity with Germany should be revived.

voices.text: When the Great Programme is complete in 1917, Russia’s peacetime army will be far larger than Germany’s. Until then Russia must gain time in every crisis, and once that day comes there is no reason to back down.
Germany and Russia have nothing to gain by fighting each other. There is no reason for Russia to bleed for the rivalry between Britain and Germany.

choices.text: As Sukhomlinov urges, speed the railways and the Great Programme with French loans, and promise the generals no retreat next time
choices.why: Once 1917 has passed, time will be on Russia’s side
choices.after: The generals were relieved, and in Berlin Moltke again received reports that by 1917 Russia would be an opponent no one could touch.

choices.text: As Durnovo advises, negotiate a new trade treaty with Germany and open talks with Austria on spheres of influence in the Balkans
choices.why: When monarchies fight each other, only revolutionaries win
choices.after: Warnings were heard in Paris that Russia was drifting away from the alliance, and the Pan-Slavs whispered that the German-born Empress was behind it.

choices.text: Keep rearmament on schedule, but with the Duma’s help put your energy into Krivoshein’s land reform and legislation for workers
choices.why: Only a country strong at home can weather the next crisis
choices.after: For the first time in years the Duma joined hands with the government, and Krivoshein prepared a bill to speed up land reform. Whether revolution was inevitable, no one can yet say.

note.text: In 1913 Russia promised France that, in return for annual loans, it would build strategic railways to its western frontier. France hoped those railways would speed Russia’s mobilization and squeeze Germany from east and west.

SR-01.title: Serbia Alone
SR-01.event: On receiving Russia’s reply, the Serbian government held an all-night cabinet meeting at Niš. The Serbian army has already begun to mobilize, and the capital, Belgrade, lies within range of the Austrian batteries across the Sava.
SR-01.scene: Spalajković comes to the Foreign Ministry and reads out a telegram from Pašić: even if the capital must be given up, Serbia cannot retreat without a fight. Since the spring of 1914 Pašić’s government has been at odds with the secret society inside the army, the Black Hand, so it can hardly order the army to lay down its arms merely on Russia’s word. In London Grey says he will try to persuade Vienna if Russia calms Serbia, and on the morning of 28 July Wilhelm in Berlin read Serbia’s reply and wrote that the cause for war had now vanished, but St Petersburg does not know this. How far Russia can hold Serbia back is the question of the night.

voices.text: Serbia respects Russia’s advice. But if Serbia gives up its capital without a fight, the army will not obey the government, and there are already officers who call the government cowards.

If Serbia takes up the sword, Vienna will advance as if it had been waiting for nothing else, and Russia will again have to choose between mobilization and surrender. This time Belgrade must be made to follow Russia’s word.

choices.text: Take up Grey’s proposal for an ambassadors’ conference at once, and again urge Serbia to entrust its fate to the Powers’ judgment
choices.why: Only at the Powers’ table can both Serbia and Russia survive
choices.after: Grey replied that he would convene an ambassadors’ conference at once. Pašić reluctantly agreed to pull the army back from Belgrade into the interior, and Vienna, mindful of the Powers’ eyes upon it, began looking for a course other than a declaration of war.

choices.text: Make Belgrade obey: tell Pašić that if he ignores Russia’s advice, Russia will withdraw its diplomatic support as well
choices.why: Serbia’s sword must not be allowed to drag Russia into war
choices.after: The Serbian government gave way before Russia’s warning, but among the officers at Niš there was talk that Russia had sold Serbia out again, as in 1909. The army’s anger turned on Pašić and the Regent.

choices.text: As Spalajković pleads, do not stop Serbia from fighting, while Russia quietly prepares mobilization of the southern districts
choices.why: Neither stop nor help the brother nation, and play for time
choices.after: Serbia decided to fight alone, and at noon on 28 July Austria declared war. Russia stayed still on the German frontier and prepared to mobilize only in the south.

note.text: In the spring of 1914 the army and Pašić’s government clashed bitterly over the administration of newly won Macedonia, and on 24 June King Peter handed the regency to Crown Prince Alexander. The Serbian government never fully controlled Apis, head of military intelligence, or the Black Hand.

HP-01.title: Russia Without General Mobilization
HP-01.event: On 31 July Austria-Hungary ordered general mobilization, including the Russian frontier. In Berlin Moltke demanded the proclamation of a ‘state of imminent danger of war’, but as long as Russia stays still on the German frontier, Bethmann Hollweg is putting off the decision.
HP-01.scene: Russia is holding out without general mobilization on the German frontier. Yanushkevich reports that with only partial mobilization in the south, or none at all, the Warsaw military district has been left defenseless, and that now Austria has ordered general mobilization, every hour that passes puts Russia at a greater disadvantage. Sazonov says this is Germany’s last chance to restrain Vienna and asks to wait one more day for Berlin’s answer. Even as you walk with the children in the gardens of Peterhof, the telephone does not stop ringing.

voices.text: The Warsaw military district is exposed to both Germany and Austria. If Your Majesty does not order general mobilization today, tomorrow will already be too late.
As long as Russia does not move on the German frontier, Berlin has a reason to restrain Vienna. Wait just one more day, Your Majesty.

choices.text: As Sazonov urges, make no move on the German frontier, and watch for one more day whether Berlin holds Vienna back
choices.why: Only if Russia stays still will Berlin have reason to restrain Vienna
choices.after: A day passed and Germany did not mobilize. This time Bethmann Hollweg pressed Vienna in earnest to ‘halt in Belgrade’.

choices.text: Heed Yanushkevich’s warning that with Austria fully mobilized Russia cannot wait longer, and switch to general mobilization
choices.why: The Warsaw district cannot be left defenseless any longer
choices.after: General mobilization notices went up in the streets of the capital. When news came that Russia had finally gone over to general mobilization, Berlin at once prepared an ultimatum.

note.text: When Austria-Hungary actually ordered general mobilization on 31 July, much of its army was already heading toward Serbia. Conrad faced great confusion in turning those forces toward the Russian front.

HP-02.title: Berlin’s Proposal

telegram.text: German government to Russian government / Austria to halt advance after occupying Belgrade / Serbia’s territorial integrity promised / Four-power mediation accepted / Condition: Russia to halt extension of mobilization

HP-02.scene: With Russia staying still on the German frontier, Bethmann Hollweg pressed Vienna and at last obtained concessions. Austria says it will advance no further after occupying Belgrade, will take no Serbian territory, and will accept mediation by the Great Powers. But there is a condition: it will not leave Belgrade until Serbia has carried out the demands. The Pan-Slav newspapers call it Russia’s shame that Serbia has lost its capital.

voices.text: As long as the points that infringe Serbia’s sovereignty remain, this proposal is only half a solution.
Britain sees only one way out: mediation, with Belgrade held as a pledge. If Russia accepts it, Britain will help guarantee the outcome.

choices.text: Agree with Grey that mediation over a pledged Belgrade is the only way out: accept Germany’s offer and a four-power conference
choices.why: Even half a solution is better than going to war
choices.after: An ambassadors’ conference opened in London, and the Austrian army halted its advance at Belgrade. In mid-August the reservists of Russia’s southern districts began to go home.

choices.text: Insist, as Sazonov does, that Austria leave Belgrade before any negotiation, since the points against Serbia’s sovereignty remain
choices.why: Negotiate with the capital in enemy hands and Serbia becomes a protectorate
choices.after: Negotiations stalled for several days and tension on the frontier rose again. Grey shuttled between the two sides and barely managed to fix a date for the conference.

choices.text: Accept the offer, but propose that disputes over the points touching Serbia’s sovereignty go to the Hague court of arbitration
choices.why: Leave the hardest issue to the judgment of the law
choices.after: Britain and Italy backed Russia’s proposal, and Vienna reluctantly agreed. The Austrian army stayed in Belgrade to await the ruling.

note.text: The Permanent Court of Arbitration, created at the Hague Peace Conference of 1899, was a body for settling disputes between states by arbitration, but it could take up a case only with the consent of all parties.

HP-03.title: The Emperor Who Sheathed the Sword
HP-03.scene: There has been no great European war, but at Peterhof pressure of another kind is building. Grand Duke Nicholas Nikolaevich and the officers of the Guard murmur that the Emperor abandoned Serbia, and nationalists in the Duma demand Sazonov’s resignation. Alexei, who turned ten on 12 August, suffers from an illness that can lay him low after the slightest injury, and the Empress wants to bring the convalescent Rasputin to the capital.

voices.text: The army will not forget this. If Your Majesty backs down again next time, I cannot vouch for the officers’ loyalty.
It is fortunate that war was avoided. Now, if the price is not to be paid at home, Your Majesty must join hands with the Duma.

choices.text: Move the Great Programme up to 1916 and speed the railways with larger French loans, to appease the Grand Duke and the officers
choices.why: The army’s loyalty must be won back with armaments
choices.after: The Great Programme, due for completion in 1917, was brought forward to 1916. On hearing the news, Moltke in Berlin was all the more convinced that time was not on Germany’s side.

choices.text: Promise Grand Duke Nicholas Nikolaevich never to back down in the next crisis, and give your patronage to Pan-Slav societies
choices.why: An emperor who retreats twice will lose his army
choices.after: The generals were satisfied, but tension persisted in Europe, where the next crisis could break out at any moment.

choices.text: As Krivoshein urges, replace the hard-line ministers and join with the Duma, putting the country’s strength into reform, not war
choices.why: The price of avoiding war must be paid in reform
choices.after: Rodzianko, President of the Duma, welcomed the Emperor’s decision, and the court hard-liners turned their backs on him. Whether Russia could have escaped revolution, no one can say for certain.

note.text: Alexei was born on 12 August 1904 (30 July Old Style). His hemophilia was a state secret, and it was the main reason the Empress relied on Rasputin.

UL-01.title: An Empire in Retreat
UL-01.scene: Just before noon, Sazonov handed Pourtalès Russia’s answer. Berlin stopped the signing of the mobilization order, and Moltke is furious that the opportunity has slipped away. But the Austrian army keeps advancing into Serbia, and the Serbian government, now at Niš, asks what Russia will do next. Ambassador Paléologue protests that France has been left alone in the face of German threats, and among the officers of the Guard the phrase ‘a second 1909’ is going around.

voices.text: Russia put its ally in danger and then retreated on its own. Paris will not easily forget this.
This is not the end. Russia cannot stand by and watch Serbia vanish from the map.

choices.text: Having retreated once, do not widen the fight: urge Serbia to accept a truce and mediation, and let it end with Belgrade occupied
choices.why: Let Serbia hold out longer and it will vanish from the map
choices.after: Pašić accepted the truce. The Austrian army remained in Belgrade and northern Serbia, and the Great Powers began discussing Serbia’s future in London.

choices.text: At least keep Serbia on the map, as Sazonov urges: warn Vienna that Russia will move again if Serbia’s independence is harmed
choices.why: Even in retreat, a line must be drawn that cannot be crossed
choices.after: Vienna could not ignore the warning and halted its advance south of Belgrade. But Germany, complaining that Russia was making threats once again, stayed on its guard.

note.text: In July 1914 more than 100,000 workers (130,000 to 150,000, by some accounts) took part in strikes in the factory districts of St Petersburg, and barricades went up in the Vyborg district around the time of Poincaré’s stay. The memoirs of the Bolshevik Duma deputy Badayev date this to 22 July. The strikes subsided once the war began.

UL-02.title: The Price of Humiliation
UL-02.scene: War has been avoided, but Russia’s prestige has sunk to its lowest point. Sazonov has resigned, and French newspapers ask what use the alliance with Russia is. Nationalists and liberals in the Duma attack the government together, and the generals say that by 1917, when the Great Programme is complete, not even Germany will be able to treat Russia lightly. Krivoshein says it is time to strengthen the country at home, but warns that if Russia backs down once more, the dynasty will not survive.

voices.text: The people may put up with Russia backing down twice, but not three times.
This affair has opened the way to joining hands with Germany again. When monarchies fight each other, only the revolutionaries win.

choices.text: As the generals urge, speed up the Great Programme and renew the French alliance, building the strength not to retreat again
choices.why: A third retreat is one the dynasty would not survive
choices.after: France responded with a new loan, and the strategic railways to the western frontier were almost finished by 1916. Tension persisted in Europe, where the next crisis could break out at any moment.

choices.text: As Durnovo advises, conclude a trade treaty with Germany and reconcile with Austria by dividing Balkan spheres of influence
choices.why: Siding with Germany rather than France is safer for the dynasty
choices.after: Berlin welcomed it, but Paris and London stopped trusting Russia, and the Triple Entente effectively collapsed.

choices.text: Strengthen the home front, as Krivoshein urges: rearm on schedule, but allow a cabinet responsible to the Duma
choices.why: Only if Emperor and Duma join hands can revolution be avoided
choices.after: For the first time since 1905, the Emperor and the Duma joined hands. The court hard-liners and the Empress objected strongly.

note.text: Durnovo’s February 1914 memorandum argued that Russia must not be dragged into the rivalry between Britain and Germany. Whether Nicholas II actually read it, however, is not confirmed.

epilogues.A: Nicholas II had kept the peace that summer, and Pan-Slavs and generals denounced him as ‘the Emperor who backed down’; but Serbia kept its independence and Russia pressed on with the Great Programme aimed at 1917. The danger of revolution that Durnovo had warned of did not go away, however. The workers who had built barricades in the capital in July 1914, the peasants who wanted land, and the deep mistrust between the Emperor and the Duma all remained. Whether, without the war, the Romanov dynasty would have survived through reform or fallen some other way is a question historians cannot answer.
epilogues.B: Russia avoided a great war at the price of standing by while Serbia’s capital was occupied. The humiliation of backing down again, after 1909, fed the anger of the Pan-Slavs and the army, and Sazonov would have found it hard to keep his post. France began to ask once more whether Russia was an ally it could rely on. In the July crisis as it actually unfolded, the memory of 1909 weighed heavily in the resolve of Russia’s leaders never to back down again.
epilogues.E: In August 1914 Russia took the offensive in East Prussia and Galicia at once, but lost its Second Army at Tannenberg, and in 1915 it suffered the Great Retreat, giving up Poland. In September 1915 Nicholas II made himself Supreme Commander and left for Stavka; the influence of the Empress and Rasputin, who remained in the capital, grew, and in December 1916 Rasputin was murdered by aristocrats. In March 1917, amid the February Revolution in Petrograd, Nicholas abdicated aboard the imperial train halted at Pskov. The family was held at Tsarskoe Selo and Tobolsk and then confined in the Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, and on the night of 16–17 July 1918, in its cellar, Nicholas and Alexandra, Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia, and thirteen-year-old Alexei were shot together with four people who had stayed with them to the end, among them their physician, Botkin. The defeat and revolution that Durnovo had warned of in his memorandum of February 1914 had come to pass.
epilogues.F: Having come through the crisis of 1914, Russia built strategic railways with French loans and moved toward completing the Great Programme. But when the next crisis came, Germany’s generals believed they had to fight before Russia grew any stronger, and Russia’s generals had resolved never to back down again. A war between still larger armies might have been even more destructive than the one that actually came, and the danger of revolution that Durnovo had warned of remained.

dossier.t: You were born in May 1868, on the feast of St Job, and came to the throne in 1894 at 26, when your father, Alexander III, died suddenly; in July 1914 you are 46. As heir, in 1891, you were wounded in the head by a policeman’s sword at Ōtsu in Japan, and in 1904–1905 you lost a war against that same Japan, and with it your fleet at Tsushima. In 1905, at the end of a revolution that began with ‘Bloody Sunday’ in the capital, you had to issue the October Manifesto and grant a Duma. You keep a diary every day, but it records mostly the weather, walks, kayaking, tennis and time with your family rather than politics. You are deeply religious, and some see in you a fatalism that accepts enduring hardship as your appointed lot.

Empress Alexandra, from the grand ducal house of Hesse in Germany, is a granddaughter of Queen Victoria and a cousin of Wilhelm II. Your mother, Maria Feodorovna, a Danish princess by birth, is the aunt of King George V of Britain, so you and George V are cousins too. Because of her son’s illness the Empress leans heavily on Grigori Rasputin, a pilgrim of Siberian peasant stock, and in the first half of 1914 Rasputin spent several evenings with the imperial family. Your father’s cousin, Grand Duke Nicholas Nikolaevich, is highly respected in the army, and his wife Anastasia and Militsa, wife of his brother Grand Duke Peter, are daughters of the King of Montenegro. Hartwig, the minister in Belgrade, was said to have influenced even Sazonov’s Balkan policy through his old colleagues in the Foreign Ministry.

Your deepest worry is your only son, Alexei, born in 1904. His hemophilia is a state secret, and in the autumn of 1912, at the hunting lodge of Spała in Poland, he came close to bleeding to death. The memory of 1905, when defeat in war led to revolution, also weighs heavily on you. Your hopes lie in the ‘Great Programme’ of rearmament, due to be finished around 1917, and in the strategic railways being built with French loans; as the monarch who proposed the Hague Peace Conference of 1899, you want to avoid a great war. At the same time you take seriously your ministers’ warning that if Russia backs down again as in 1909, it will lose its standing in the Balkans and on the question of the Black Sea Straits.

movers.intro: Historians differ sharply over how much responsibility Nicholas II and Russia bear for the war of 1914. The main views are these.
views: Dominic Lieven explains that Russia’s leaders believed the empire’s security and great-power status would collapse if the Balkans and the Straits fell into German and Austrian hands. He holds that even an Emperor who wanted peace accepted his ministers’ judgment that Russia could not back down again as it had in 1909.

Sean McMeekin, in The Russian Origins of the First World War (2011), argued that Russia coveted the Straits and Constantinople and, by effectively bringing mobilization forward from late July, bore a large share of responsibility for the war. The argument has also drawn much criticism for overreading the sources.

Christopher Clark singles out the ‘period preparatory to war’ of 25–26 July and the general mobilization of 30 July as decisive moments that escalated the crisis. Rather than pinning the blame on one country, however, he explains the war as the result of misjudgments by leaders in several capitals, each compounding the others.

M. N. Pokrovsky and other Soviet historians of the 1920s published the tsarist government’s secret diplomatic documents and argued that imperialist aims such as control of the Straits led Russia into war.
movers.note: On the question ‘Was Serbia Russia’s puppet?’, the picture the sources give is not simple. Russia was Serbia’s chief patron and Hartwig was close to Pašić, but the Serbian government could not control the Black Hand, the secret society within the army. In his 1917 statement Apis wrote that he decided on the assassination after hearing from the Russian military attaché Artamonov that Russia would not abandon Serbia, and that he received money for intelligence work from Artamonov but did not tell him of the assassination plan itself; how far the statement can be trusted is disputed. On 24 July the Russian Council of Ministers advised Serbia not to resist by force, and when Sazonov repeatedly demanded in August and September that part of Macedonia be ceded to Bulgaria, Pašić attached conditions that amounted to a refusal.
